title: Termination: structural recursion and fuel
objective: Judge statements about why v0 needs no fuel, how fuel makes a runner total, what an out-of-fuel result means, and why goldens need definitions the kernel can reduce.

blocks.md: Lean accepts a function only if it can see that the function stops. That raises a question for any evaluator: what stops it?

choice.prompt: A fueled runner returns `outOfFuel` after 1,000 steps. What do you know about the program?

options.why: More fuel may let it finish.

options.text: Only that no verdict was reached within 1,000 steps.
options.why: Like `unknown` in Stage 1, it is no verdict, and it fails closed.
A long run is not an error.

blocks.md:
A function that could loop forever would let you prove false things. If `bad n = bad n + 1` were accepted, subtracting `bad n` from both sides would prove `0 = 1`. So every Lean definition passes a termination check, and there are two ways through. In **structural recursion** each recursive call is on a smaller piece of the input, and Lean sees that by itself. The kernel can also run such a definition by plain unfolding. In **well-founded recursion** you name a measure that shrinks, and Lean proves it does. The definition then stays opaque to the kernel's own evaluation, so it is not necessarily equal to its value by computation.

Mini-Plinth v0 sits in the easy case. A command body is one statement, and `exec` recurses on the syntax of expressions, so it is structural and needs no fuel. That is why a golden, `theorem g : exec p c s = r := by decide`, can be decided: the kernel computes the left side.

blocks.direction: The replay shows what Lean says to each `decide`.

code.text:
def countdown : Nat → Nat
  | 0 => 0
  | n + 1 => countdown n

def countdownWF (n : Nat) : Nat :=
  if n = 0 then 0 else countdownWF (n - 1)
termination_by n

theorem g0 : countdown 3 = 0 := by decide
theorem g : countdownWF 3 = 0 := by decide

call.prompt: `theorem g : countdownWF 3 = 0 := by decide`, where `countdownWF` uses well-founded recursion. What happens?

options.why: `decide` needs the kernel to compute the value, and a well-founded definition need not reduce.

options.text: It fails: the equation is false.
options.why: The equation is true. Reduction failed, not the equation.

options.text: It fails to reduce: no verdict.
options.why: The kernel cannot unfold the definition, so it says nothing about the equation.

blocks.after: `countdown` is structural, so `decide` succeeds on it. `countdownWF` is not reduced {{run:RUN-lean-golden-harness}}. A golden that stops here has established nothing.

blocks.md: Some programs would not fit the structural mould, such as a loop you add later. For those the runner takes **fuel**, a counter that drops at every step. At zero it stops with `outOfFuel`, so the runner is total by construction. `outOfFuel` is no verdict. It says the bound ran out, not that the program loops, and it is not an error the program raised. Your own system has the same shape: a request that times out tells you the deadline passed, not whether the work would have finished.
A counted loop outside v0, run with two bounds.

code.text:
inductive Run where
  | done (n : Nat)
  | outOfFuel
  deriving DecidableEq

def runFuel : Nat → Nat → Run
  | 0, _ => .outOfFuel
  | fuel + 1, n => if n = 0 then .done 0 else runFuel fuel (n - 1)

theorem fuel3   : runFuel 3 10 = .outOfFuel := by decide
theorem fuel100 : runFuel 100 10 = .done 0 := by decide

call.prompt: With fuel 3 the runner says `outOfFuel`, and with fuel 100 it finishes. Did the program's meaning change?

options.text: No: fuel bounds the runner, not the program.
options.why: The same program gets two different bounds.

options.text: Yes: with fuel 3 it is a failing program.
options.why: A bound that is too small is not a defect of the program.

blocks.after: Only the bound changed. A bigger one can turn `outOfFuel` into an answer, and a golden whose right side is `outOfFuel` records the bound.

options.text: v0 needs no fuel: every body is one statement and `exec` recurses on the syntax.
options.why: One statement per body and recursion on syntax need no counter.

options.text: `outOfFuel` is an error the program raised.
options.why: The runner raised it, because its bound ran out.

options.text: A golden whose right side is `outOfFuel` states a fact about the program.
options.why: It states a fact about a bound, which a larger one could change.

options.text: A well-founded `exec` lets `decide` check goldens as well as a structural one does.
options.why: The kernel may fail to reduce it, so a golden could end in no verdict.

choice.prompt: A golden `theorem g : exec p c s = r := by decide` fails because your `exec` uses well-founded recursion and the kernel cannot reduce it. What kind of result is this?

options.text: A failed golden: the equation is false.
options.why: The equation may well be true. Nothing was computed.

options.text: No verdict: nothing is established either way.
options.why: The kernel could not compute either side, so the golden proves nothing.

options.text: A passing golden: Lean reported no mismatch.
options.why: A check that does not run is not a check that passes.

blocks.md: Read 2026-10-23. Lean Language Reference, section 7.6.2 "Structural Recursion" and section 7.6.3 "Well-Founded Recursion", which says that well-founded applications are not necessarily definitionally equal to their return values. Check the numbering against the Lean version you use.
